# HOW WE WORK APART
## Coordination latency and communication quality as two separate decisions

**Operating decision paper | v1.0**
*(Team-level playbooks, meeting templates and the instrumentation spec are Annexes A–F. Annex G — vendor comparison — is not required for this decision.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of the two-track diagnosis, the async-default operating model, the time-zone fairness rule in §4.3, the decision-rights model in §6.2, the conflict ladder in §7, the metric set in §11, and **funding for a 90-day Gate 0 pilot on three teams**. Global rollout becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

"Our distributed teams have communication problems" is two problems, not one, and they take opposite treatments. **Coordination latency** — work waiting on someone in another time zone — is an *architecture* problem, fixed by removing cross-time-zone dependencies, moving decision rights down, and making handoffs self-sufficient. **Communication quality** — misunderstanding, unspoken disagreement, silent dissent surfacing three weeks late as a defect — is a *norms and language* problem, fixed by codifying what is currently intuited, and by removing the fluency and status penalties that make speaking up expensive. Treating latency with better communication produces more meetings and slower work. Treating misunderstanding with better tooling produces well-documented confusion. We therefore propose two tracks with different owners, different clock speeds, and different success metrics (§2). Both tracks rest on one structural choice: **written-first, asynchronous by default, with synchronous time reserved for the three things it is actually superior at** — deciding contested questions, repairing relationships, and building trust with new people (§3). We also make one distributional commitment: time-zone burden is never zero, someone always pays it, and unmeasured it silently lands on the least powerful region and shows up eighteen months later as attrition. §4.3 makes the payer explicit and rotates them. Two claims here are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that our delays are predominantly dependency-structural rather than behavioural, and that our misunderstanding rate is concentrated at specific cultural and language interfaces rather than distributed evenly. Gate 0 exists to measure exactly those two things, and §13.2 states in advance what result would flip the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, evidence, and the cost rule

### 0.1 How to read the figures

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Working-time law, rest-period rules, works council consultation duties, data residency, statutory holidays, recording/monitoring consent law | Should be *certain* — verify, never assume | Gate 0, by employment counsel per jurisdiction |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Current cycle time, blocked hours, meeting load per FTE, off-hours meeting distribution, rework rate, safety scores | Instrumentable from existing systems: ±[10]%. **Self-reported culture and safety data: ±[30]% and biased optimistic** | Gate 0, by instrumentation + pulse survey |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Overlap window length, decision SLA, meeting-hours cap, travel cadence | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by this committee |

Anything touching off-hours work expectations, monitoring, recording, or scheduling outside contracted hours is **[V]**. In several of our jurisdictions these are not policy preferences; they are statutory or works-council matters, and a globally uniform rule may be unlawful in some locations. §12.4 prices that.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out |
|---|---|
| How distributed project teams communicate, decide, hand off, and disagree | Which projects we run; portfolio prioritisation |
| Time-zone architecture and its fairness | Return-to-office policy for co-located staff |
| Cultural and language fluency infrastructure | Compensation banding by geography |
| Conflict prevention, detection and resolution | Formal grievance/HR investigations (interfaces with §7.5, does not replace) |
| Manager capability for distributed leadership | Reorganisation of reporting lines |
| Instrumentation and metrics | Tool procurement (Gate 1) |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every practice proposed here carries a stated cost — in hours, in delay, or in someone's evening.** Written-first costs writing time. Overlap windows cost someone their morning or their dinner. Decision records cost the author twenty minutes. Rotation costs consistency. A practice listed without its cost has not been thought through and will be abandoned within two quarters when the cost arrives unannounced.

Baseline, to be confirmed at Gate 0: [~1,900] engineers and PMs across [11] countries and [6] primary time-zone clusters **[R]**; median project team size [9]; median spread [7.5] hours between the earliest and latest member **[R]**; [31]% of team members work in a language other than their first **[R]**.

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How do we communicate better across time zones? | Which of our delays are caused by *needing* to communicate across time zones at all — and can that need be designed out? |
| How do we make people aware of cultural differences? | Which specific behaviours are currently being *interpreted* rather than *specified* — and what would it cost to specify them? |
| How do we resolve conflicts faster? | Why is disagreement surfacing late and hot instead of early and cheap — and what is making early dissent expensive for the person who has it? |

**Corollary 1 — a meeting is not communication, it is a purchase.** It is bought with attention hours multiplied by headcount, plus the fragmentation cost to everyone's remaining day, plus — for at least one region — sleep or family time. A recurring 45-minute meeting with 9 attendees costs ~[290] person-hours a year **[D]** before fragmentation. It should be justified like any other recurring spend, and cancelled like one.

**Corollary 2 — the cheapest handoff is the one that doesn't happen.** One removed cross-time-zone dependency saves more cycle time than any improvement in how well that dependency is communicated. Architecture beats etiquette.

**Corollary 3 — silence is data, and it is usually the most expensive data we ignore.** In a distributed team, non-response is ambiguous: it may mean agreement, absence, disagreement that is culturally expensive to voice, or a message never seen. Systems that cannot distinguish these four produce confident, false consensus.

---

## §2 Diagnosis before prescription: the two tracks

### 2.1 The failure modes are structurally different

| | **Track A — Coordination latency** | **Track B — Communication quality** |
|---|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Work waits. "Blocked pending review from Bangalore." A two-day question takes nine days. | Work is done wrong. Rework. "That's not what I asked for." Late-surfacing objections. |
| **Root cause** | Dependency structure, centralised decision rights, non-self-sufficient handoffs, unclear ownership | Unstated norms, high/low-context mismatch, fluency asymmetry, status/safety asymmetry, ambiguous written artefacts |
| **Clock speed** | Improves in weeks once dependencies are cut | Improves in quarters; it is capability-building, not policy |
| **Failure mode if untreated** | Schedule slip, WIP accumulation, heroics by a few individuals | Defects, rework, quiet attrition, distrust between regions |
| **Failure mode if mistreated** | "More sync meetings" → burnout in the off-set region, no latency gain | "More tooling/training" → well-documented, well-attended confusion |
| **Owner** | Engineering/Delivery leadership (structural authority) | People/Team leads + team-level charters (normative authority) |
| **Primary metric** | Handoff wait time; decision cycle time (§11.1) | Rework rate; dissent latency; safety score (§11.2) |

**Do not fuse these.** The single most common failure in this domain is a "global collaboration programme" that buys a tool, runs a cultural-awareness workshop, adds two ceremonies, and measures nothing — thereby treating a structural problem with normative instruments and a normative problem with procurement.

### 2.2 What we do *not* yet know

Our current evidence is anecdotal and escalation-driven, which biases it toward the loudest teams and the most senior complainants. Before designing at scale we need to know the split: **what fraction of observed delay is dependency-structural versus behavioural?** Our working hypothesis is [60/40] **[R]**, tested at Gate 0. If it is [20/80], Track A shrinks to a minor workstream and this paper is substantially rewritten (§13.2).

### 2.3 The attention budget

Distributed-work improvement competes with delivery for the same manager hours. We cap it:

| Group | Hours/week to this programme | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Team leads (pilot teams) | [3.0] | Reduced meeting load (§3.4), not added on top |
| Programme lead | [40] (dedicated, 1 FTE) | New, funded |
| Regional champions ([6]) | [4.0] | Reallocated from existing "engagement" duties |
| Team members (pilot) | [1.5] | Reduced meeting load |

If the meeting-hours reduction in §3.4 does not materialise, this programme is a net add to load and must be re-scoped, not absorbed.

## §3 The operating model: async by default, sync by exception

### 3.1 The four modes, and what each is actually for

Most dysfunction comes from using the wrong mode. Specify the mode, not just the channel.

| Mode | Use it for | Never use it for | Latency expectation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Broadcast** (docs, wikis, changelogs, recorded demos) | Context, status, decisions already made, reference | Anything needing a reply | No reply expected; read within [3] business days |
| **2. Asynchronous discussion** (threads, doc comments, PR review, RFC) | Proposals, review, structured debate, most questions | Anything urgent; anything emotionally loaded | Reply within **[24] working hours**, ack within [8] |
| **3. Synchronous scheduled** (calls, workshops) | Contested decisions, kickoff, design divergence, relationship repair, brainstorming | Status reporting; information transfer that could be written | Real time; **always produces a written artefact within [12]h** |
| **4. Synchronous urgent** (page, call-now) | Production incident, active customer harm, legal/safety | Impatience; a manager's preferred latency | Immediate; **strictly rate-limited and audited** |

**The default is Mode 2.** Escalation to Mode 3 requires a reason that survives being written down. Mode 4 has a monthly audit: if a team uses it more than [2]×/month outside incidents, that is a Track A finding, not an individual failing.

**Cost of this model:** writing is slower than talking for the author and faster for everyone else. Expect a [10–20]% productivity dip in weeks 1–6 as people learn to write. Budget it; do not treat it as failure.

### 3.2 Written-first is a skill, not a policy

Mandating documentation without teaching it produces long, unreadable documents that nobody reads, which is worse than no documentation because it manufactures the illusion of shared context.

**We fund the capability:**
- A [90]-minute "writing for decisions" module: BLUF (bottom line up front), one-screen summaries, explicit ask, explicit deadline, explicit non-goals.
- **Template enforcement over prose freedom.** Templates (Annex A) reduce the fluency penalty on non-native writers dramatically — they replace "compose an argument in a second language" with "fill defined fields."
- A **[400]-word cap** on any document expecting a same-day response. Longer documents get longer SLAs.
- **Plain-language standard:** no idioms, no sports or military metaphors, no regional humour in decision artefacts, expand acronyms on first use per document. This is not political; idioms are the single highest-density source of cross-cultural misreading, and they are free to remove.

### 3.3 The self-sufficient handoff

The core Track A instrument. A handoff crossing a time-zone boundary must be answerable without the sender. Required fields (Annex B):

1. **What I did** — 3 bullets max
2. **What I need from you** — one sentence, imperative, one recipient named
3. **Decision or input?** — explicit
4. **By when, and what happens if not** — real consequence, not "ASAP"
5. **What I already tried / considered and rejected** — prevents the round trip
6. **If you disagree with my approach, the alternative I'd accept is X** — pre-authorises a decision without a second cycle
7. **If blocked, escalate to [named person] in your own time zone**

Field 6 is the highest-leverage item in this paper. It converts a two-cycle exchange (question → answer → action, ~[36]h) into one (~[14]h) and simultaneously grants the receiver agency instead of an instruction.

### 3.4 Meeting reform (the funding source for everything else)

We are buying the hours for this programme from existing meetings, not adding hours.

| Rule | Effect |
|---|---|
| **No agenda + no pre-read + no named decision → auto-cancelled** | Removes ~[15]% of recurring meetings **[R]** |
| **Status meetings are abolished** and replaced by written updates (Mode 1) | Removes ~[20]% **[R]** |
| **Default 25/50 minutes**, not 30/60 | Returns [17]% of remaining meeting time as recovery/transition |
| **Every meeting has a written artefact** posted within [12]h, including decisions, owners, and *dissent recorded by name or by "none voiced"* | Makes absentees non-penalised; makes silence visible |
| **Recording + transcript + summary default-on**, subject to **[V]** consent law per jurisdiction | Removes attendance-by-fear; a major fairness gain for off-set regions |
| **Meeting-hours cap:** [10]h/week for ICs, [16]h for leads | Forcing function; breaches are a systems signal |

**Cost to the core:** some information genuinely does transfer better in conversation, and some relationships are maintained by low-value meetings. Expect complaints in month 1–2, principally from managers who use meetings as their status-visibility instrument. §9.2 gives them a replacement.

### 3.5 Response-time contracts (removes the ambiguity of silence)

Every team publishes, in its charter:

| Channel | Acknowledge | Substantive response |
|---|---|---|
| Decision request (tagged) | [8] working hours | [24] working hours |
| Code/design review | [12] working hours | [24] working hours |
| General question | [24] working hours | [3] business days |
| Broadcast/FYI | None | None |

**"Working hours" means the responder's, not the sender's.** A message sent at 18:00 CET is not late at 09:00 IST the next day; it is on time. This single definition eliminates a large share of perceived unresponsiveness, which is very often just time-zone arithmetic misread as disrespect **[R]**.

**And the reciprocal obligation:** if you cannot meet the SLA, say so within the acknowledgement window. "Can't get to this until Thursday" is a complete and acceptable answer. Silence is not.

---

## §4 Time-zone architecture

### 4.1 Choose a topology deliberately

| Topology | How it works | Best for | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Overlap-core** | Every team has [3–4]h of common hours daily; async outside it | Teams with high interdependence and ≤[6]h spread | Constrains hiring geography; compresses the day |
| **Follow-the-sun** | Deliberate handoff between regions to run [16–24]h/day | Incident response, ops, well-specified pipelines | **Poor for creative/design work**; handoff overhead often exceeds the gain |
| **Ownership-boundary (recommended default)** | Cut the *work* along time-zone lines so each region owns end-to-end deliverables; interfaces are contracts, not conversations | Most product/engineering teams | Requires real architectural and organisational discipline |
| **Hub-and-satellite** | One dominant region decides; others execute | Nothing we should be doing | Creates permanent second-class regions; the primary driver of the attrition and disengagement we are seeing **[R]** |

**Recommendation:** default to **ownership-boundary**, with a **[3]-hour overlap core** as a floor for genuinely coupled teams **[D]**. Follow-the-sun only where the work is specifiable in advance (incident response, build/release, monitored operations).

**Diagnostic to run at Gate 0:** for each pilot team, count cross-time-zone dependencies per sprint. If the number exceeds [4], the problem is the team's *shape*, not its communication habits. Reshape before retraining.

### 4.2 Split-team spread limits

A team spread over [12]+ hours has, structurally, no overlap and must operate at [100]% async — which is achievable but requires the strongest documentation discipline we have. A team spread over [4–8] hours is in the worst position: enough overlap to be tempting, not enough to be sufficient, so it defaults to synchronous habits that quietly cost one region their evenings.

**Rule [D]:** for new teams, either cluster within [5] hours, or design explicitly for full-async at [10]+ hours. Avoid the middle unless the interdependence genuinely requires it.

3. **Cap it.** No individual exceeds [4] off-hours meeting-hours per month **[D]** without their lead's documented consent and a compensating adjustment.

## The recommendation in one paragraph

Expansion into "a new region" is two decisions, not one. **Demand entry** and **supply entry** have different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different owners; fusing them into a single geography is how mid-sized brands lose margin in both. We propose a **Demand Track** entering **Japan** as beachhead — chosen on the scored criteria in §3.2, not asserted — with **South Korea opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5); and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam** as a new manufacturing origin while retaining **Portugal and Turkey** as nearshore replenishment and **India as a source of certified organic fibre and yarn only**. We enter as a **provable-longevity** brand — garments sold with their own evidence and their own repair — at a price architecture that never competes with either (§4). ## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, lead-time inventory, defect rate and audit overhead** — and does the preference actually apply to *our* bill of materials? |

# HOW WE WORK APART
## Coordination latency and communication quality as two separate decisions

**Operating decision paper | v1.0**
*(Team-level playbooks, meeting templates and the instrumentation spec are Annexes A–F. Annex G — vendor comparison — is not required for this decision.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of the two-track diagnosis, the async-default operating model, the time-zone fairness rule in §4.3, the decision-rights model in §6.2, the conflict ladder in §7, the metric set in §11, and **funding for a 90-day Gate 0 pilot on three teams**. Global rollout becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

"Our distributed teams have communication problems" is two problems, not one, and they take opposite treatments. **Coordination latency** — work waiting on someone in another time zone — is an *architecture* problem, fixed by removing cross-time-zone dependencies, moving decision rights down, and making handoffs self-sufficient. **Communication quality** — misunderstanding, unspoken disagreement, silent dissent surfacing three weeks late as a defect — is a *norms and language* problem, fixed by codifying what is currently intuited, and by removing the fluency and status penalties that make speaking up expensive. Treating latency with better communication produces more meetings and slower work. Treating misunderstanding with better tooling produces well-documented confusion. We therefore propose two tracks with different owners, different clock speeds, and different success metrics (§2). Both tracks rest on one structural choice: **written-first, asynchronous by default, with synchronous time reserved for the three things it is actually superior at** — deciding contested questions, repairing relationships, and building trust with new people (§3). We also make one distributional commitment: time-zone burden is never zero, someone always pays it, and unmeasured it silently lands on the least powerful region and shows up eighteen months later as attrition. §4.3 makes the payer explicit and rotates them. Two claims here are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that our delays are predominantly dependency-structural rather than behavioural, and that our misunderstanding rate is concentrated at specific cultural and language interfaces rather than distributed evenly. Gate 0 exists to measure exactly those two things, and §13.2 states in advance what result would flip the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, evidence, and the cost rule

### 0.1 How to read the figures

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Working-time law, rest-period rules, works council consultation duties, data residency, statutory holidays, recording/monitoring consent law | Should be *certain* — verify, never assume | Gate 0, by employment counsel per jurisdiction |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Current cycle time, blocked hours, meeting load per FTE, off-hours meeting distribution, rework rate, safety scores | Instrumentable from existing systems: ±[10]%. **Self-reported culture and safety data: ±[30]% and biased optimistic** | Gate 0, by instrumentation + pulse survey |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Overlap window length, decision SLA, meeting-hours cap, travel cadence | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by this committee |

Anything touching off-hours work expectations, monitoring, recording, or scheduling outside contracted hours is **[V]**. In several of our jurisdictions these are not policy preferences; they are statutory or works-council matters, and a globally uniform rule may be unlawful in some locations. §12.4 prices that.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out |
|---|---|
| How distributed project teams communicate, decide, hand off, and disagree | Which projects we run; portfolio prioritisation |
| Time-zone architecture and its fairness | Return-to-office policy for co-located staff |
| Cultural and language fluency infrastructure | Compensation banding by geography |
| Conflict prevention, detection and resolution | Formal grievance/HR investigations (interfaces with §7.5, does not replace) |
| Manager capability for distributed leadership | Reorganisation of reporting lines |
| Instrumentation and metrics | Tool procurement (Gate 1) |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every practice proposed here carries a stated cost — in hours, in delay, or in someone's evening.** Written-first costs writing time. Overlap windows cost someone their morning or their dinner. Decision records cost the author twenty minutes. Rotation costs consistency. A practice listed without its cost has not been thought through and will be abandoned within two quarters when the cost arrives unannounced.

Baseline, to be confirmed at Gate 0: [~1,900] engineers and PMs across [11] countries and [6] primary time-zone clusters **[R]**; median project team size [9]; median spread [7.5] hours between the earliest and latest member **[R]**; [31]% of team members work in a language other than their first **[R]**.

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How do we communicate better across time zones? | Which of our delays are caused by *needing* to communicate across time zones at all — and can that need be designed out? |
| How do we make people aware of cultural differences? | Which specific behaviours are currently being *interpreted* rather than *specified* — and what would it cost to specify them? |
| How do we resolve conflicts faster? | Why is disagreement surfacing late and hot instead of early and cheap — and what is making early dissent expensive for the person who has it? |

**Corollary 1 — a meeting is not communication, it is a purchase.** It is bought with attention hours multiplied by headcount, plus the fragmentation cost to everyone's remaining day, plus — for at least one region — sleep or family time. A recurring 45-minute meeting with 9 attendees costs ~[290] person-hours a year **[D]** before fragmentation. It should be justified like any other recurring spend, and cancelled like one.

**Corollary 2 — the cheapest handoff is the one that doesn't happen.** One removed cross-time-zone dependency saves more cycle time than any improvement in how well that dependency is communicated. Architecture beats etiquette.

**Corollary 3 — silence is data, and it is usually the most expensive data we ignore.** In a distributed team, non-response is ambiguous: it may mean agreement, absence, disagreement that is culturally expensive to voice, or a message never seen. Systems that cannot distinguish these four produce confident, false consensus.

---

## §2 Diagnosis before prescription: the two tracks

### 2.1 The failure modes are structurally different

| | **Track A — Coordination latency** | **Track B — Communication quality** |
|---|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Work waits. "Blocked pending review from Bangalore." A two-day question takes nine days. | Work is done wrong. Rework. "That's not what I asked for." Late-surfacing objections. |
| **Root cause** | Dependency structure, centralised decision rights, non-self-sufficient handoffs, unclear ownership | Unstated norms, high/low-context mismatch, fluency asymmetry, status/safety asymmetry, ambiguous written artefacts |
| **Clock speed** | Improves in weeks once dependencies are cut | Improves in quarters; it is capability-building, not policy |
| **Failure mode if untreated** | Schedule slip, WIP accumulation, heroics by a few individuals | Defects, rework, quiet attrition, distrust between regions |
| **Failure mode if mistreated** | "More sync meetings" → burnout in the off-set region, no latency gain | "More tooling/training" → well-documented, well-attended confusion |
| **Owner** | Engineering/Delivery leadership (structural authority) | People/Team leads + team-level charters (normative authority) |
| **Primary metric** | Handoff wait time; decision cycle time (§11.1) | Rework rate; dissent latency; safety score (§11.2) |

**Do not fuse these.** The single most common failure in this domain is a "global collaboration programme" that buys a tool, runs a cultural-awareness workshop, adds two ceremonies, and measures nothing — thereby treating a structural problem with normative instruments and a normative problem with procurement.

### 2.2 What we do *not* yet know

Our current evidence is anecdotal and escalation-driven, which biases it toward the loudest teams and the most senior complainants. Before designing at scale we need to know the split: **what fraction of observed delay is dependency-structural versus behavioural?** Our working hypothesis is [60/40] **[R]**, tested at Gate 0. If it is [20/80], Track A shrinks to a minor workstream and this paper is substantially rewritten (§13.2).

### 2.3 The attention budget

Distributed-work improvement competes with delivery for the same manager hours. We cap it:

| Group | Hours/week to this programme | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Team leads (pilot teams) | [3.0] | Reduced meeting load (§3.4), not added on top |
| Programme lead | [40] (dedicated, 1 FTE) | New, funded |
| Regional champions ([6]) | [4.0] | Reallocated from existing "engagement" duties |
| Team members (pilot) | [1.5] | Reduced meeting load |

If the meeting-hours reduction in §3.4 does not materialise, this programme is a net add to load and must be re-scoped, not absorbed.

---

## §3 The operating model: async by default, sync by exception

### 3.1 The four modes, and what each is actually for

Most dysfunction comes from using the wrong mode. Specify the mode, not just the channel.

| Mode | Use it for | Never use it for | Latency expectation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Broadcast** (docs, wikis, changelogs, recorded demos) | Context, status, decisions already made, reference | Anything needing a reply | No reply expected; read within [3] business days |
| **2. Asynchronous discussion** (threads, doc comments, PR review, RFC) | Proposals, review, structured debate, most questions | Anything urgent; anything emotionally loaded | Reply within **[24] working hours**, ack within [8] |
| **3. Synchronous scheduled** (calls, workshops) | Contested decisions, kickoff, design divergence, relationship repair, brainstorming | Status reporting; information transfer that could be written | Real time; **always produces a written artefact within [12]h** |
| **4. Synchronous urgent** (page, call-now) | Production incident, active customer harm, legal/safety | Impatience; a manager's preferred latency | Immediate; **strictly rate-limited and audited** |

**The default is Mode 2.** Escalation to Mode 3 requires a reason that survives being written down. Mode 4 has a monthly audit: if a team uses it more than [2]×/month outside incidents, that is a Track A finding, not an individual failing.

**Cost of this model:** writing is slower than talking for the author and faster for everyone else. Expect a [10–20]% productivity dip in weeks 1–6 as people learn to write. Budget it; do not treat it as failure.

### 3.2 Written-first is a skill, not a policy

Mandating documentation without teaching it produces long, unreadable documents that nobody reads, which is worse than no documentation because it manufactures the illusion of shared context.

**We fund the capability:**
- A [90]-minute "writing for decisions" module: BLUF (bottom line up front), one-screen summaries, explicit ask, explicit deadline, explicit non-goals.
- **Template enforcement over prose freedom.** Templates (Annex A) reduce the fluency penalty on non-native writers dramatically — they replace "compose an argument in a second language" with "fill defined fields."

- **Plain-language standard:** no idioms, no sports or military metaphors, no regional humour in decision artefacts, expand acronyms on first use per document. This is not political; idioms are the single highest-density source of cross-cultural misreading, and they are free to remove.

### 3.3 The self-sufficient handoff

The core Track A instrument. A handoff crossing a time-zone boundary must be answerable without the sender. Required fields (Annex B):

1. **What I did** — 3 bullets max
2. **What I need from you** — one sentence, imperative, one recipient named
3. **Decision or input?** — explicit
4. **By when, and what happens if not** — real consequence, not "ASAP"
5. **What I already tried / considered and rejected** — prevents the round trip
6. **If you disagree with my approach, the alternative I'd accept is X** — pre-authorises a decision without a second cycle
7. **If blocked, escalate to [named person] in your own time zone**

Field 6 is the highest-leverage item in this paper. It converts a two-cycle exchange (question → answer → action, ~[36]h) into one (~[14]h) and simultaneously grants the receiver agency instead of an instruction.

### 3.4 Meeting reform (the funding source for everything else)

We are buying the hours for this programme from existing meetings, not adding hours.

| Rule | Effect |
|---|---|
| **No agenda + no pre-read + no named decision → auto-cancelled** | Removes ~[15]% of recurring meetings **[R]** |
| **Status meetings are abolished** and replaced by written updates (Mode 1) | Removes ~[20]% **[R]** |
| **Default 25/50 minutes**, not 30/60 | Returns [17]% of remaining meeting time as recovery/transition |

| **Meeting-hours cap:** [10]h/week for ICs, [16]h for leads | Forcing function; breaches are a systems signal |

### 3.5 Response-time contracts (removes the ambiguity of silence)

Every team publishes, in its charter:

| Channel | Acknowledge | Substantive response |
|---|---|---|
| Decision request (tagged) | [8] working hours | [24] working hours |
| Code/design review | [12] working hours | [24] working hours |
| General question | [24] working hours | [3] business days |
| Broadcast/FYI | None | None |

| **Hub-and-satellite** | One dominant region decides; others execute | Nothing we should be doing | Creates permanent second-class regions; the primary driver of the attrition and disengagement we are seeing **[R]** |

### 4.2 Split-team spread limits

# Critique: "HOW WE WORK APART" (Operating decision paper v1.0)

## 1. Blocking defect: the document is incomplete

The text terminates mid-word in §4.3 item 4 ("...or works counc"). Beyond that, **§5 through §13 do not exist**, yet the paper's own "Decision sought" asks the committee to approve:

- the decision-rights model in **§6.2** — missing
- the conflict ladder in **§7** — missing
- the metric set in **§11** — missing

It also forward-references §7.5, §9.2, §12.4 and §13.2 (the falsification criteria, explicitly promised in the opening paragraph as the paper's integrity guarantee). A decision paper that requests approval of six artefacts and delivers three cannot be actioned.

More seriously for the brief: **the original request names three deliverables — communication, collaboration, conflict resolution — and conflict resolution is entirely absent.** What exists is a well-built communication-architecture paper with a promissory note where a third of the answer should be.

## 2. Cultural diversity is under-served relative to the brief

"Culturally diverse" is one of two adjectives in the request. The paper touches it four times: high/low-context mismatch (one cell in a table), fluency asymmetry, idiom removal (§3.2), and status/safety asymmetry. Absent:

- **Power distance** and its effect on whether a junior engineer in one region will contradict a senior architect in another — the direct cause of the "silent dissent surfacing three weeks later" the paper opens with.
- **Commitment language.** "Yes" as acknowledgement vs. agreement; "that will be difficult" as refusal. This is the single highest-frequency source of missed deadlines in multi-region teams and is not mentioned.
- **Feedback norms** (direct/indirect, public/private, positive-sandwich vs. plain), which is where most cross-regional interpersonal friction originates.
- **Face** and the cost of public correction — directly relevant to §3.4's "dissent recorded by name."
- **Calendars**: statutory holidays, religious observance, differing weekend days (Fri–Sat in some markets), month-long holiday periods. §4.3 addresses hour-of-day fairness but not day-of-year, which breaks sprint planning routinely.
- **Anti-essentialism guardrail.** The paper correctly rejects cultural-awareness workshops as a substitute for structure, but offers no replacement mechanism for building cultural literacy — leaving a vacuum that teams will fill with nationality stereotypes. "Specify the behaviour rather than train the awareness" is a good principle but is only delivered for idioms and templates.
- **Language support** beyond templates: no interpretation, no clarification-without-penalty norm, no turn-taking discipline on calls (where fast native speakers structurally dominate), no captioning, no glossary of internal terms.

## 3. Internal contradictions

**(a) The topology recommendation contradicts the spread rule.** §4.1 recommends a **3-hour overlap core** as the floor for coupled teams. A 3-hour overlap implies roughly a 5–7 hour spread. §4.2 then declares 4–8 hours "the worst position" and instructs teams to avoid it. The paper's own baseline states median spread is **7.5 hours** — i.e., the median team sits in the band the paper tells us to avoid, while the recommended overlap-core design puts it there deliberately. Either resolve the two rules or state explicitly that the median team must be restructured (and cost that — hiring geography, transfers, works-council implications).

**(b) Asserted causality on data the paper says it doesn't have.** §2.2: "our current evidence is anecdotal and escalation-driven." §4.1: hub-and-satellite is "the primary driver of the attrition and disengagement we are seeing **[R]**." That is a causal claim about attrition, tagged as researchable, presented as established. Downgrade to a hypothesis with a Gate 0 test.

**(c) "Non-negotiable" fairness rule that is negotiable by law.** §4.3 is headed "non-negotiable"; §0.1 and §3.4 concede that off-hours expectations, recording and monitoring are statutory/works-council matters that may make a uniform rule unlawful. Reframe as: the *principle* is non-negotiable; the *instrument* is jurisdiction-variable, with a named fallback per cluster.

**(d) SLA table mismatch.** §3.1 sets Mode 2 substantive reply at [24] working hours; §3.5 sets "general question" at [3] business days. Same channel, two numbers.

## 4. Quantitative apparatus is partly theatre

The [V]/[R]/[D] tagging is a genuine strength inherited from the prior paper, but it is applied unevenly and in places incorrectly:

- **Empty placeholders in the load-bearing rule.** §4.3 states "[%] of recurring cross-regional meetings fall outside 08:00–18:00 for APAC, versus [%] EMEA and [%] AMER." Three blanks in the sentence that justifies the entire fairness section. Either supply illustrative figures with a clear "illustrative" flag or restructure the sentence so it doesn't depend on numbers that don't exist.
- **Tag-type error.** "~[290] person-hours a year **[D]**" is not a design target; it is arithmetic (0.75h × 9 × ~44 weeks ≈ 297). Tagging a calculation as a *choice we are making* undermines the taxonomy's whole point.
- **Invented baseline.** [~1,900] engineers, [11] countries, [31]% non-native speakers — the agent has no basis for any of these. Brackets signal placeholder status, but a reader will absorb them as scale assumptions. State once, prominently, that the baseline block is a worked illustration to be replaced.
- **Unsourced leverage claim.** §3.3: Field 6 "converts a two-cycle exchange (~[36]h) into one (~[14]h)" and is "the highest-leverage item in this paper" — untagged, underived, and asserted superlatively.

## 5. The funding logic does not close

§3.4 is titled "the funding source for everything else," and §2.3 caps effort on the basis that lead/member hours come out of reduced meeting load. But no reconciliation is shown: removing ~15% + ~20% of *recurring* meetings, plus 17% of remaining *duration*, is never converted into hours per lead per week and set against the 3.0 h/wk and 1.5 h/wk demands. The 17% duration saving is also double-counted — §3.4 itself says it is "returned as recovery/transition," which means it is not available to fund the programme. And the "Decision sought" requests **funding for a 90-day pilot without ever naming an amount** — a conspicuous omission given the source-format precedent of a specific figure.

## 6. Unaddressed risks

- **The instrumentation is a surveillance system.** Blocked hours, meeting load per FTE, off-hours attendance per person, response-SLA compliance, recording default-on. Deployed without an explicit data-minimisation commitment (aggregate-only reporting, no individual dashboards, no performance-management use, retention limits, GDPR/works-council basis), this measurably *reduces* the psychological safety Track B exists to raise. The paper should pre-empt this in a dedicated clause, not leave it to §12.4.
- **Ownership-boundary topology can entrench regional silos.** Cutting work along time-zone lines so "interfaces are contracts, not conversations" reduces cross-regional contact — the mechanism by which trust and cohesion are built, and an explicit goal in the brief ("team cohesion"). This is a real trade-off the recommendation ignores. It also risks each region acquiring a monoculture and a stereotype of the others.
- **Async escalation.** Mode 2 must never be used for "anything emotionally loaded," but conflict routinely *originates* async (a terse PR comment, a review rejection at 03:00). There is no rule for detecting and moving a heating thread to Mode 3 — the most common real-world conflict trigger in distributed engineering.
- **Manager incentives.** §3.4 correctly predicts resistance from managers who use meetings for status visibility, but no change to promotion criteria, performance review, or manager selection for distributed competence is proposed. Without that, the model reverts.
- **No rollout mechanics:** pilot-team selection criteria, timeline, RACI beyond an "Owner" column, anti-backslide mechanism, or explicit stop conditions.

## 7. Smaller items

- §2.3 "reallocated from existing 'engagement' duties" — the scare quotes are snide and pre-judge the value of work being displaced; also 6 champions for 11 countries / 6 clusters gives no coverage logic.
- §3.2's [400]-word cap conflicts with §3.3's seven-field handoff template plus §3.4's artefact requirements; specify which artefacts the cap binds.
- "No regional humour" is unenforceable and reads as sterilising; narrow it to decision artefacts (as intended) and say so unambiguously.
- §4.1 dismisses hub-and-satellite as "nothing we should be doing" without acknowledging that regulatory proximity, customer presence or acquisition history sometimes mandate it — and without a transition path for teams currently in it.

## 8. What works and should be preserved

The two-track diagnosis (latency = architecture, quality = norms) is a genuinely strong organising idea and the paper's main contribution. Also excellent: Corollary 3 (silence as ambiguous data); "working hours means the responder's, not the sender's"; recording dissent by name *or* "none voiced"; the self-sufficient handoff template; OHLI as a published metric at delivery-metric visibility; the §0.3 cost rule; and the advance commitment to falsification conditions. The mode taxonomy (§3.1) is the cleanest such table I have seen in this genre.

## Priority fixes

1. **Write §5–§13.** Conflict resolution (§7) is a named deliverable of the brief and is entirely missing: task/process/relationship conflict distinction, early-dissent mechanisms, disagree-and-commit, a named escalation ladder with timeframes and neutral cross-regional facilitation, trust repair, and the HR/grievance interface.
2. **Add a substantive cultural-interface section**: power distance, commitment language, feedback norms, face, calendars, language support, anti-essentialism guardrail.
3. **Resolve the §4.1/§4.2 overlap-vs-spread contradiction** and state the consequence for the median 7.5-hour team.
4. **Fill or restructure the empty [%] placeholders** in §4.3 and correct the [D]/[R] mis-tagging.
5. **Close the funding arithmetic** and name a pilot budget figure.
6. **Add a data-ethics clause** covering monitoring, aggregation, and non-use in performance management.
7. **Add a cohesion-risk clause** on ownership-boundary siloing, plus the trust-building/co-location cadence the tag table promises but never delivers.

# HOW WE WORK APART
## Coordination latency and communication quality as two separate problems

**Operating decision paper | v2.0**
*(Team-level playbooks, meeting and artefact templates, the instrumentation spec and the jurisdiction matrix are Annexes A–H. Annex I — tool/vendor comparison — is deliberately excluded from this decision; see §14.5.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of (1) the two-track diagnosis and its separated ownership (§2), (2) the async-default operating model (§3), (3) the time-zone architecture bands and the fairness principle in §4.3, (4) the cultural-interface layer in §5, (5) the decision-rights model in §6.2, (6) the conflict ladder in §7, (7) the data-ethics guardrails in §10, (8) the metric set in §11, and (9) **€[420]k plus €[60]k contingency to fund a 90-day Gate 0 diagnostic pilot on three teams** (§13.4). Global rollout becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1. Nothing in this paper commits us to a tool purchase, a reorganisation, or a change to any employment contract.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

"Our distributed teams have communication problems" is two problems, not one, and they take opposite treatments. **Coordination latency** — work waiting on someone in another time zone — is an *architecture* problem, fixed by removing cross-time-zone dependencies, pushing decision rights down, and making handoffs self-sufficient. **Communication quality** — misunderstanding, unspoken disagreement, dissent that surfaces three weeks late as a defect — is a *norms, language and safety* problem, fixed by specifying what is currently intuited and by removing the fluency and status penalties that make speaking up expensive. Treating latency with better communication produces more meetings and slower work. Treating misunderstanding with better tooling produces well-documented confusion. We therefore propose two tracks with different owners, clock speeds and success metrics (§2). Both rest on one structural choice: **written-first, asynchronous by default, with synchronous time reserved for the four things it is genuinely superior at** — deciding contested questions, diverging on design, repairing relationships, and building trust with people we do not yet know (§3). On top of that sits a **cultural-interface layer** (§5) that converts cultural difference from something we ask people to be "aware" of into something we *specify*: how commitment is expressed, how objection is registered, how feedback is delivered, whose calendar is authoritative, and who carries the burden of clarity in a shared second language. We make one distributional commitment: time-zone burden is never zero, someone always pays it, and unmeasured it silently lands on the region with the least organisational power and returns eighteen months later as attrition — §4.3 makes the payer visible and rotates them. And we accept one uncomfortable trade-off openly: the topology that best cuts latency also cuts cross-regional contact, which is how cohesion is built; §8 buys that cohesion back deliberately rather than pretending the tension away. Three claims here are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that our delays are predominantly dependency-structural rather than behavioural; that our misunderstanding rate is concentrated at identifiable interfaces rather than distributed evenly; and that off-hours burden is unevenly distributed by region. Gate 0 exists to measure exactly those three things, and **§13.2 states in advance what result would flip this recommendation.**

---

## §0 Scope, evidence, and the cost rule

### 0.1 How to read the figures

Three kinds of number appear in this paper, tagged on first use.

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Working-time law, rest-period rules, works-council consultation duties, data-residency rules, statutory holidays, recording/monitoring consent law | Should be *certain* — verify, never assume | Gate 0, by employment counsel per jurisdiction |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Cycle time, blocked hours, meeting load per FTE, off-hours meeting distribution, rework rate, dissent latency, safety scores | Instrumentable from systems we already own: ±[10]%. **Self-reported culture and safety data: ±[30]% and biased optimistic** | Gate 0, by instrumentation + pulse survey |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Overlap-window length, decision SLA, meeting-hours cap, travel cadence, rotation period | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by this committee |
| **[C]** | **Calculation** | Person-hour cost of a recurring meeting; funding reconciliation in §3.6 | Arithmetic — correct if its inputs are; inputs carry their own tag | Recomputed at Gate 0 with real inputs |

**[C] is new in v2.0** because v1.0 tagged arithmetic as design intent, which is exactly the confusion the taxonomy exists to prevent. A calculation is not a choice.

Anything touching off-hours work expectations, monitoring, recording, or scheduling outside contracted hours is **[V]**. In several of our jurisdictions these are not policy preferences; they are statutory or works-council matters, and **a globally uniform rule may be unlawful in some locations.** §12 prices that and names the per-cluster fallback.

### 0.2 The baseline block is an illustration, not a finding

> **Read this once and remember it.** The figures in the box below are a **worked illustration** used to make the arithmetic in this paper checkable. They are not measurements. Every one of them is replaced at Gate 0 by instrumented data, and every downstream number recomputes. Bracketed numbers elsewhere follow the same convention.

**Illustrative baseline [R], to be replaced at Gate 0:**
[~1,900] engineers and PMs; [11] countries; [6] primary time-zone clusters; median project-team size [9]; median spread [7.5] hours between earliest and latest member; [31]% of team members working in a language other than their first; median lead meeting load [18]h/week, median IC [12]h/week; [~70]% of meeting hours recurring rather than ad hoc.

### 0.3 In scope / out of scope

| Time-zone architecture and its fairness | Return-to-office policy for co-located staff |

### 0.4 The rule of this document

**Every practice proposed here carries a stated cost — in hours, in delay, in consistency, or in someone's evening.** Written-first costs authoring time. Overlap windows cost someone their morning or their dinner. Decision records cost the author twenty minutes. Rotation costs continuity. Ownership-boundary topology costs cross-regional contact. A practice listed without its cost has not been thought through and will be abandoned within two quarters, when the cost arrives unannounced. Each section below carries an explicit **Cost** line.

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How do we communicate better across time zones? | Which of our delays are caused by *needing* to communicate across time zones at all — and can that need be designed out? |
| How do we make people aware of cultural differences? | Which specific behaviours are currently being *interpreted* rather than *specified* — and what would it cost to specify them? |
| How do we resolve conflicts faster? | Why is disagreement surfacing late and hot instead of early and cheap — and what makes early dissent expensive for the person who holds it? |

**Corollary 1 — a meeting is not communication, it is a purchase.** It is bought with attention-hours × headcount, plus the fragmentation cost to everyone's remaining day, plus — for at least one region — sleep or family time. A recurring 45-minute meeting with 9 attendees costs 0.75 × 9 × [44] working weeks ≈ **[297] person-hours a year [C]** (inputs: duration and headcount observed **[R]**; 44 weeks assumed net of leave **[D]**), *before* fragmentation. It should be justified like any other recurring spend, reviewed annually, and cancelled like one.

**Corollary 2 — the cheapest handoff is the one that doesn't happen.** One removed cross-time-zone dependency saves more cycle time than any conceivable improvement in how well that dependency is communicated. Architecture beats etiquette. But see Corollary 4.

**Corollary 3 — silence is data, and it is the most expensive data we currently discard.** In a distributed team non-response is ambiguous: it may mean assent, absence, disagreement that is culturally or hierarchically expensive to voice, or a message never seen. A system that cannot distinguish those four manufactures confident, false consensus. §3.5 and §5.3 exist to disambiguate silence.

**Corollary 4 — contact is not overhead, it is the substrate.** Every dependency we remove also removes an occasion for two regions to learn each other's competence and constraints. Latency reduction and cohesion pull in opposite directions. We therefore purchase cohesion explicitly (§8) rather than hoping it survives the efficiency programme. A paper that only optimises latency will deliver fast, cold, mutually suspicious regions.

---

## §2 Diagnosis before prescription: the two tracks

### 2.1 The failure modes are structurally different

| | **Track A — Coordination latency** | **Track B — Communication quality** |
|---|---|---|
| **Symptom** | Work waits. "Blocked pending review from Bengaluru." A two-day question takes nine days. | Work is done wrong. Rework. "That is not what I asked for." Objections surfacing after commitment. |
| **Root cause** | Dependency structure, centralised decision rights, non-self-sufficient handoffs, unclear ownership, undesigned overlap | Unstated norms, high/low-context mismatch, commitment-language mismatch, fluency asymmetry, power-distance and face asymmetry, ambiguous artefacts |
| **Clock speed** | Weeks, once dependencies are cut | Quarters; it is capability-building and trust-building, not policy issuance |
| **Cost if untreated** | Schedule slip, WIP accumulation, heroics by a few individuals, single points of failure | Defects, rework, quiet attrition, region-vs-region distrust, reputational damage inside the company |
| **Cost if *mistreated*** | "More sync meetings" → burnout in the off-set region, no latency gain | "More tooling and awareness training" → well-documented, well-attended confusion, plus new stereotypes |
| **Owner** | VP Engineering / Delivery (structural authority: can change team shape, interfaces, decision rights) | Chief People Officer + team leads (normative authority: charters, capability, safety) |
| **Primary metric** | Handoff wait time; decision cycle time (§11.1) | Rework rate; dissent latency; safety score (§11.2) |
| **Escalation route if the two conflict** | Joint sponsor pair; unresolved conflicts go to the COO with a written option paper (§14.3) |

**Do not fuse these.** The characteristic failure in this domain is a "global collaboration programme" that buys a tool, runs a cultural-awareness workshop, adds two ceremonies, and measures nothing — treating a structural problem with normative instruments and a normative problem with procurement.

### 2.2 What we do *not* yet know

Our current evidence is anecdotal and escalation-driven, which biases it toward the loudest teams and the most senior complainants. Three splits must be measured before we design at scale:

| Question | Working hypothesis **[R]** | If wrong |
|---|---|---|
| What fraction of observed delay is dependency-structural vs behavioural? | [60/40] | At [20/80], Track A shrinks to a minor workstream and this paper is substantially rewritten (§13.2) |
| Is misunderstanding concentrated at identifiable interfaces (specific region pairs, specific language pairs, specific role pairs) or distributed evenly? | Concentrated: top [3] interfaces carry [>50]% of rework attributable to miscommunication | If evenly distributed, §5 becomes universal capability-building rather than targeted interface work — slower and more expensive |
| Is off-hours burden unevenly distributed by region? | Yes, materially, against APAC | If burden is roughly even, §4.3's rotation machinery is unnecessary overhead and we keep only the measurement |

### 2.3 The attention budget
